name: NH4SH ice (no visible optical constants are published)
paper: the estimate's inputs: C. and M. Cuthbertson, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. Lond. A 213 (1914) 1–26, DOI 10.1098/rsta.1914.0001, for NH3's and HCl's dispersions; C. and M. Cuthbertson, Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A 83 (1910) 171–176, DOI 10.1098/rspa.1910.0003, for H2S's; C. D. West, "The crystal structures of some alkali hydrosulfides and monosulfides", Z. Kristallogr. 88 (1934) 97–115, DOI 10.1524/zkri.1934.88.1.97, for NH4SH's cell; C. P. Gopalakrishnan, "The thermo-optic behaviour of calcium fluoride, ammonium chloride and zinc-blende at low temperatures", J. Indian Inst. Sci. 39 (1957) 8–12, eq. 7, for NH4Cl's dispersion as G. Poinsot and J.-P. Mathieu measured it (Ann. Phys. (Paris) 12e sér., 10 (1955) 481–486, DOI 10.1051/anphys/195510010481); H. E. Swanson and E. Tatge, Standard X-ray Diffraction Powder Patterns, NBS Circular 539, vol. 1 (1953), pp. 59–61, for NH4Cl's cell
source: a Lorentz–Lorenz estimate, not a measurement (science-r08-nonspherical.md §3.1, ruled 2026-10-10): the molar refraction of NH3 plus H2S from their gas dispersions as stated at 0 °C and 760 mm (view/atmosphere/rayleigh.ts's Cuthbertson rows, each at the density its paper reduces to: Z = 0.998136 for NH3 and 1.000657 for H2S), raised by NH4Cl's ionic increment of 2.7% (its n_D 1.6391, from Gopalakrishnan 1957's fit to Poinsot and Mathieu 1955's dispersion, and 1.5258 g cm⁻³, from the X-ray cell of NBS Circular 539 (Pm3̄m, a = 3.8756 Å at 26 °C, one formula unit), against NH3 and HCl from Cuthbertson 1914 at 589.3 nm, 2.68%; science-r08-gases-2.md §2), over the molar volume of West 1934's cell as the Crystallography Open Database gives it, entry 1010249, https://www.crystallography.net/cod/1010249.cif, SHA-256 e721ed9fed41cab1c267ecadd4de31692340d3bfcefd6d9183312ae3a746bb71, fetched 2026-10-10 (P4/nmm, a = 6.011 Å, c = 4.009 Å, two formula units: 43.62 cm³ mol⁻¹, 1.1717 g cm⁻³). The cell is as published, at room temperature and possibly in kX units, about ±0.005 in n. The gas dispersions are measured over 480–670.8 nm (NH3) and 486.1–656.3 nm (H2S) and extrapolated beyond. No visible optical constants of NH4SH are published: Howett et al. 2007 (JOSA B 24, 126) measured it only over 1,300–12,000 cm⁻¹ (0.83–7.7 µm). The stated band spans an ionic increment from 0 to +12%. The same estimate for NH3 ice, at the cell of I. Olovsson and D. H. Templeton (Acta Cryst. 12 (1959) 832; COD 2310927; a = 5.138 Å, four molecules), gives 1.465 against the 1.436 at 550 nm that Martonchik et al. 1984 measure (Appl. Opt. 23, 541). k = 0, since pure NH4SH is a white solid (PubChem CID 25515, from ICSC); the colours it takes on Jupiter come from radiolysis products (Loeffler and Hudson 2018, Icarus 302, 418). It replaces the earlier stand-in of 1.80, which Sromovsky et al. 2017 (Icarus 291, 232, §4.3) state without a source, after the best-fit effective index of 1.85 that Sato et al. 2013 (Icarus 222, 100) find for Jupiter's clouds, a fit that particle shape and size trade against. 1.80 would need a molar refraction 22% above the additive one.
licence: estimated values from cited constants and CC0 crystal data (the Crystallography Open Database's entry 1010249); no data set is copied (decision-r08-licences.md row 5)
reduction: n = √((1 + 2x) ÷ (1 − x)), with x the raised molar refraction over the molar volume, evaluated on 380–780 nm every 5 nm to six significant figures; k = 0
standIn: a non-absorbing particle whose real index is a Lorentz–Lorenz estimate, 1.674 at 380 nm, 1.638 at 550 nm and 1.623 at 780 nm, within +0.081 and -0.022, since no visible optical constants are published
